title: When do you break a design principle on purpose?
summary: One of the clearest senior-vs-mid signals in the room — a real, deliberate violation and the reasoning that made it the right call.

slides.markdown:
This closes out the principles bank because it's the synthesis question — it assumes you know the principles well enough to know when following one literally is the wrong move. "I never break principles" reads as rigid, not disciplined; the strong answer names a real violation, the constraint that justified it, and what was done instead.

The senior signal isn't the violation itself — plenty of people break principles by accident — it's the *reasoning* that made it deliberate.

slides.sectionTitle: Clarifying question: hypothetical, or a real story?
slides.markdown:
Ask **"do you want a hypothetical example, or a real story from my own work?"** If you have a genuine one, always prefer it — a real story with real constraints (deadline, team size, a specific measured cost) is far more convincing than a plausible-sounding hypothetical, and it's much harder to fake under follow-up questions.

If you don't have one ready, say so honestly and reason through a concrete scenario live rather than pretend it's real.

slides.sectionTitle: The answer skeleton: name the principle, the constraint, and what you did instead
slides.markdown:
Three explicit parts, always. **Name the principle** you deliberately didn't follow. **Name the constraint** that made following it worse — team size, timeline, actual measured cost of the "correct" version. **Name what you did instead**, and be honest that it's a trade-off, not a free win.

The skeleton itself demonstrates the judgment being tested — it's the same cost-first reasoning from resolving conflicting principles, applied to breaking one outright rather than choosing between two.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: a deliberately "impure" method mixing I/O and logic
slides.markdown:
```python
def process_refund(order_id):
    # deliberately not split into fetch/validate/apply/notify —
    # this endpoint has exactly one caller, changes twice a year, and
    # a 3-person team; splitting added three files for no real benefit
    order = db.fetch_order(order_id)
    if order.status != "delivered":
        raise ValueError("can't refund undelivered order")
    order.status = "refunded"
    db.save(order)
    mailer.send(order.user.email, "Your refund was processed")
```
This mixes data access, validation, and notification in one function — a clear SRP violation by the book — kept that way on purpose because splitting it produced three files a three-person team had to jump between for a function that changes twice a year.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: by-the-book vs pragmatic, at this team's actual size
slides.markdown:
| | By-the-book (split into 4 classes) | Pragmatic (kept as one function) |
|---|---|---|
| Files to navigate for one change | 4 | 1 |
| Actors currently driving change | 1 (the whole team, together) | 1 (the whole team, together) |
| Change frequency | Twice a year | Twice a year |
| Cost paid | Navigation overhead with no isolation payoff | A slightly larger function, explicitly justified |

How to decide: the by-the-book version's theoretical benefit (isolating independent actors) doesn't exist here — there's only one actor — so its cost is pure overhead.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: how do you know this wasn't just laziness dressed up as pragmatism?
slides.markdown:
The honest test: could you name the cost you're accepting *before* being asked to justify it, or only after? A deliberate trade-off comes with the cost already named at decision time — "I'm accepting worse navigability for this specific function because it's low-churn and single-owner." Laziness dressed up as pragmatism only produces that justification retroactively, when challenged.

A second test: would you make the same call again on a similar case, or was this a one-off excuse that happened to work out? Consistency across similar situations is evidence of a real principle, not an after-the-fact rationalization.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: would you make the same call in a codebase ten times bigger?
slides.markdown:
No, and saying so explicitly is important — the whole justification was scale-dependent (small team, low change frequency, single owner). At ten times the size, more actors likely touch this code, change frequency likely rises, and the navigation cost of splitting starts paying for itself in ways it doesn't at the current scale.

The strong answer treats this as an obvious "no" with the reasoning restated, not a trick question — it confirms the original call was genuinely conditional on specific facts, not a general belief that SRP doesn't matter.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: leaving a trail so the next person knows it was deliberate
slides.markdown:
A one-line comment naming the trade-off, not just the decision: `# kept as one function deliberately — low churn, single owner, see PR #452 for the split-vs-keep discussion` is far more useful than silence, and more useful than a vague `# TODO: refactor this someday`.

The goal is that the *next* engineer — possibly at a different team size, possibly after this function's change frequency has gone up — can tell the constraints that justified this call, and re-evaluate them explicitly rather than either blindly preserving or blindly "fixing" a decision they don't have context for.

**Weak belief:** always following every principle to the letter is itself the mark of good engineering, and deviating from one is a failure to avoid.

**Why it's weak:** it reads as rigid and inexperienced rather than disciplined — every senior engineer has real stories of a principle costing more than it bought in a specific situation, and claiming otherwise suggests either limited experience or an unwillingness to admit trade-offs.

**Correct model:** have a real, specific story ready, with the constraint and reasoning named — not a vague "sometimes you have to be pragmatic."

slides.sectionTitle: Wrong answer: dressing up a mistake as a deliberate trade-off
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** retroactively describing a violation that was actually just an oversight — nobody thought about it at the time — as if it had been a considered trade-off from the start.

**Why it's wrong:** interviewers who probe with follow-ups ("what was the actual cost you weighed?", "would you do it again at 10x scale?") will surface the gap fast — a real trade-off has answers ready for both; a retrofitted excuse doesn't.

**Correct model:** if you don't have a genuine deliberate example, say so and reason through a live scenario instead of manufacturing a fake one.

"I kept a `process_refund` function as one method — fetching, validating, updating, and notifying all inline — which is an SRP violation by the book. The constraint: a 3-person team, a function that changes twice a year, and only one actor ever touching it. Splitting it into four classes would have added navigation overhead with no isolation benefit, since there was no second actor to isolate from. I left a comment naming the trade-off explicitly so the next person could re-evaluate it if the team or change frequency ever grows — and I'd make the opposite call in a codebase ten times bigger, since the constraints that justified this wouldn't hold anymore."

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: does team size or codebase age change the answer here too?
slides.markdown:
Yes — this question echoes the same theme as [is SRP always the right call](iv-is-srp-always-right) and [resolving conflicting principles](iv-resolving-conflicting-principles): team size and change frequency are the two variables that most often flip a principle's cost-benefit balance. A young codebase with one owner and low churn tolerates more deliberate violations than an old one with many contributors and high churn, where the same violation compounds into real risk.

Naming this connection across questions — rather than treating each principle question as an isolated case — is itself a strong signal of synthesized understanding.
